section_summaries.epidemiology: Viral gastroenteritis is a major cause of acute gastroenteritis globally, particularly in children under 5 in low-income countries, with viruses accounting for the majority of cases. Rotavirus is the single most important cause in infants and young children, prevalent worldwide, with winter seasonality in temperate countries and year-round infection in tropical areas, primarily transmitted fecal-orally. Noroviruses are leading causes of epidemic gastroenteritis across all age groups globally, highly transmissible via fecal-oral or vomitus-oral routes, and show significant genetic diversity with GII.4 strains predominating in human infections. Enteric adenoviruses (species F, serotypes 40 and 41) cause epidemic, endemic, or sporadic infections mainly in infancy and early childhood, with no seasonal preference, and are transmitted feco-orally. Astroviruses are prevalent in small children and the elderly, often showing winter peaks in temperate climates, and are spread person-to-person by the fecal-oral route. Sapovirus prevalence ranges from 2% to 12% of acute gastroenteritis cases, with early life exposure common and transmission occurring via the fecal-oral route, similar to norovirus.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Viral gastroenteritis viruses transmit feco-orally, infecting small intestine epithelial cells, causing damage to the villous epithelium, impairing fluid absorption, and leading to watery diarrhea without inflammation, as replication occurs within enterocytes without spreading into the submucosa. Rotaviruses infect duodenal mucosa, causing shortening and atrophy of intestinal villi, enterocyte vacuolization, and death, leading to osmotic diarrhea and dehydration; rotavirus non-structural protein NSP4 may act as an enterotoxin, and serotonin secretion may induce diarrhea and vomiting. Noroviruses recognize histo-blood group antigens on mucosal epithelia, with infection causing broadening and blunting of intestinal villi, crypt-cell hyperplasia, and increased epithelial barrier dysfunction resulting in leak flux; acquired immunity is not lifelong, allowing for multiple infections. Adenoviruses replicate in respiratory and gastrointestinal epithelia, with pentons being directly cytotoxic and early viral proteins counteracting host immune responses; a serotype-specific humoral immune response provides homotypic protection. Astrovirus pathogenesis involves viral replication in intestinal tissue, causing inflammatory infiltrates, villous atrophy, and decreased intestinal disaccharidase activity leading to osmotic diarrhea, with increased intestinal permeability after apical infection. Sapovirus exposure occurs early in life, but unlike rotavirus and norovirus, susceptibility is not associated with histo-blood group antigen phenotype or secretor status.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Viral gastroenteritis typically presents with acute-onset, watery, non-bloody diarrhea, often accompanied by vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain; dehydration is the most important complication. Rotavirus infection has an abrupt onset after 1-2 days incubation, causing fever, vomiting, and non-bloody watery diarrhea lasting 2-6 days, and is a leading cause of severe acute gastroenteritis in infants and young children. Norovirus infection, with a 12-48 hour incubation, causes acute-onset watery, non-bloody diarrhea and/or vomiting lasting 1-3 days, sometimes with nausea, abdominal cramps, headache, and chills, and can be severe in young children, the elderly, and hospitalized patients. Enteric adenovirus-associated diarrhea is similar to other viral causes but may last longer (3-11 days), with common fever and vomiting, and watery non-bloody stools; adenoviruses are also isolated in cases of intussusception. Astrovirus gastroenteritis is generally milder, with headache, nausea, low-grade fever, and vomiting, an incubation of about 3 days, and illness typically lasting 3-5 days. Sapovirus infection begins abruptly after 1-3 days incubation with watery, non-bloody diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain, usually less severe than rotavirus, though it can cause severe disease in vulnerable populations.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Etiologic diagnosis of viral gastroenteritis requires laboratory investigation as clinical features alone are indistinguishable. Rotavirus is diagnosed by detecting viral antigen in stool using immunologic methods (e.g., ELISA, immunochromatographic assays) or by detecting viral RNA using molecular methods like RT-PCR, with viral load cut-offs advisable. Norovirus diagnosis uses RT-PCR as the reference standard for detecting virus in stool, water, and food, providing high sensitivity and specificity, though immunoassays lack adequate sensitivity for routine clinical use; fecal specimens should be collected early. Enteric adenoviruses are detected in fecal specimens primarily by ELISA using species F-specific monoclonal antibodies or by highly sensitive PCR for viral genome detection, as cell cultures are poor for growth. Astrovirus diagnosis involves virus visualization, antigen detection (EIAs), or genome amplification (RT-PCR), with RT-PCR being the screening method of choice for epidemiologic research. Sapovirus diagnosis relies on characteristic calicivirus-like morphology under electron microscopy or definitively on reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for genome identification.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment for viral gastroenteritis is primarily supportive, focusing on oral rehydration solutions (ORS) to replace electrolytes and glucose, or intravenous rehydration therapy for severe dehydration, shock, or reduced consciousness. Dietary management, including continued breastfeeding and age-appropriate foods, is important. Zinc supplementation is recommended for children in developing countries. Anti-emetics (e.g., metoclopramide, ondansetron) and anti-motility/anti-secretory drugs are generally not recommended due to mixed results, lack of substantiation, or potential severe complications. While no specific antiviral chemotherapy or vaccine is available for norovirus, sapovirus, or astrovirus, Cidofovir has been used for disseminated adenovirus infections. Intussusception associated with adenovirus is typically managed by hydrostatic reduction (barium or air enema).
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention for viral gastroenteritis emphasizes strict hygiene measures, including handwashing, safe disposal of feces, and disinfection of contaminated surfaces, to reduce transmission. Highly efficacious live attenuated oral rotavirus vaccines (RotaTeq, Rotarix) are globally licensed and incorporated into childhood immunization schedules, substantially reducing rotavirus hospitalizations and deaths, with cross-protection against commonly circulating strains. For enteric adenoviruses, no vaccine is currently available, and public health measures to confine outbreaks include cohort nursing, use of personal protective equipment, disinfection, and exclusion of infected individuals. Norovirus vaccines are currently in clinical trials. Astrovirus prevention focuses on hygiene, and while a short-term, serotype-specific protection against re-infection has been observed, vaccines are still in development. There is no vaccine available for sapovirus.
